blocks.title: Honors — equilibrium is a claim, not a coincidence
blocks.markdown: CPA writes ΣF = 0 when an object is at rest or moving at constant velocity. Honors treats that equation as a **claim you have to defend**: *I assert the forces sum to zero, here is the evidence, here is the reasoning.* A balanced free-body diagram is the beginning of an argument, not the end of one.

## What equilibrium actually asserts

When $\Sigma \vec{F} = 0$, the acceleration is zero — *and that is the whole statement.* It does **not** say the object is at rest. A crate sliding across a floor at a steady 4 m/s is in equilibrium just as much as a crate sitting still: in both, velocity isn't changing, so the net force is zero.

This is where intuition fights you. The naive model says *'moving means there's a leftover force pushing it along.'* Equilibrium says the opposite: a thing can move forever at constant velocity with **zero** net force. The friction backward exactly cancels the push forward. To claim equilibrium, you must show **every component** sums to zero — not just the ones you happened to notice.

blocks.title: State your assumptions
blocks.markdown: An equilibrium claim is only as good as the model under it. Before you write ΣF = 0, name what you're assuming: that you've drawn **every** force (no hidden ones), that the object is a **point** (no rotation/torque to worry about), and that the surface, string, or support is **rigid** and not accelerating. If any of those breaks, your tidy ΣF = 0 breaks with it.

blocks.frame: This object IS / IS NOT in equilibrium. My evidence is ___. The assumption my claim depends on most is ___, and it would break if ___.
blocks.prompt: JUSTIFY: A sign hangs motionless from two angled cables. A classmate says 'it's not moving, so there are no forces on it.' Defend the correct equilibrium claim instead: explain what ΣF = 0 really asserts here, cite the forces that cancel, and name the one assumption your claim leans on hardest.
